Most data originated from government agency compilations, public web resources, and select journal articles. However, detailed local information on energy demand was limited. During a site visit to Puerto Rico, researchers met with multiple agencies, universities, and facilities management teams. The team at UPR-RP provided comprehensive data on building- level energy demand and existing system configurations. The modeling conducted in this study is based on those configurations. 3.2 System Configurations and Building Characteristics 3.2.1 Central Chilled Water Plant at the University of Puerto Rico at Río Piedras The UPR-RP campus has one of the largest heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning systems in Puerto Rico. Almost 7,430 tons of refrigeration (26 megawatts thermal) are required to provide air conditioning to the facilities. An increment of 3,000 tons for new buildings has been estimated. UPR-RP operates eight chilled water plants across campus, including a central chilled water plant, with a combined maximum installed cooling capacity of approximately 10,600 tons of refrigeration. The central plant distributes chilled water to about 30 buildings via three main distribution lines that serve the Facundo Bueso building, general academic buildings, and the Sports Complex (Figure 13). The plant includes key mechanical components, including water- cooled vapor-compression chillers, evaporative cooling towers, circulation pumps, chemical treatment systems, and supply and return piping loops, thus forming a distribution system for campus-wide space cooling. The campus building stock served by the central plant is functionally diverse, ranging from general-purpose academic buildings to specialized facilities, such as medical buildings, theaters, and athletic complexes. Each building has distinct operational schedules, internal load patterns, and cooling requirements, resulting in highly variable and often complex load profiles. This diversity presents a significant challenge for energy performance evaluation and system-level optimization, as no single building type can fully capture the range of operational conditions across the campus. Moreover, while design and operational cooling capacity data were collected during a site visit, measured hourly load data were not available, limiting the capability to analyze detailed energy demand, water consumption, and economic parameters. 3.3 Building Energy Modeling To address the data gap and support techno-economic analysis, this study employed a simulation-based approach to generate time-resolved cooling load profiles.
